judge_1.rationale: The exclusion from wages for small-boat fishing crew paid by catch share under §3401(a)(17) (tied to §3121(b)(20)) is still in the Code. The four-part test and crew-size rules apply to wages paid in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: The exception for fishing-boat crew paid by a share of the catch is still in force (3121(b)(20), and 3401(a)(17) for withholding). The regulation's conditions for it still apply in 2025.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes tax rules for fishing services remuneration that apply to services "performed on or after December 31, 1954" with no stated expiration date or sunset provision, and references ongoing employment tax sections (3121(b)(20)) and reporting requirements that would apply in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to services performed on or after December 31, 1954, and the evidence confirms IRC section 3121(b)(20) remains in force as of March 2025, so the fishing exemption rules operate in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §2056A(b)(12) is still in force. Under it, the QDOT estate tax stops applying when the surviving spouse becomes a citizen, and the certification and election rules apply to 2025 events. The stale §2102(c) cross-reference (now §2102(b)) does not change that.

judge_2.rationale: IRC 2056A(b)(12) is in force, and it ends the QDOT tax when the surviving spouse becomes a citizen. The regulation's notice rule and its special elections still apply. The stale 2102(c) citation does not defeat this.

reader_A.reason: The regulation clearly states operative rules governing QDOT estate tax treatment when a surviving spouse becomes a U.S. citizen, referencing currently-codified IRC sections that would remain in effect in 2025 absent legislative change.

reader_B.reason: The regulation cites statutory provisions confirmed in force as of March 2025 and contains no time-limiting language, establishing substantive rules for ongoing situations involving surviving spouses who become U.S. citizens.

judge_1.rationale: The §4161(b) excise tax on bows, their parts and accessories, and quivers/broadheads/points is still in force. These definitions (bows, parts and accessories, quivers) still decide what is taxable in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: IRC 4161(b) is in force in March 2025 and still taxes bows, archery parts and accessories, quivers and arrow shafts. The regulation's definitions of these terms still apply to manufacturers' sales.

reader_A.reason: This regulation section provides definitional rules that govern the application of the tax imposed by section 4161(b) on bows and arrows, a tax that remains in effect for taxable years beginning in 2025 absent specific legislative repeal, making these definitional rules still operative.

reader_B.reason: The regulation defines operational terms for section 4161(b) of the tax code, which the evidence confirms is in force as of March 2025, establishing these definitions as actively applicable for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This regulation implements the qualified state individual income tax provisions (§§6361-6365, subchapter E). Congress repealed them in 1990 (OBRA 1990), and the ledger shows §§6362 and 6363 as repealed. No judicial-review rule has any remaining effect.

judge_2.rationale: This rule gives judicial review of determinations under the state-administered income tax program (IRC 6361-6365, subchapter E). Those sections were repealed in 1990, and 6362 and 6363 do not appear in the March 2025 Code. No rule has any remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: This regulation concerns judicial review procedures for the State Elective Nonfederal Individual Income Tax Credit (Subchapter E), which was repealed effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, making these procedural rules inapplicable to any taxable year in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation implements sections 6362 and 6363, which have both been repealed according to the evidence file, so the stated rules cannot operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

adjudicated.rationale: IRC 52(e) is in force at 119-4. It directs regulations applying rules similar to former 46(e) and (h) to RICs, REITs and 1381(a) cooperatives when computing the section 51 work opportunity credit. 1.52-3(b) and (c)(1) are those rules; the 44B and 46 citations are stale, not repealed. Para (a) (repealed 52(e)(1)(A)) and (c)(2) (pre-1978) no longer apply.

judge_1.rationale: The limits apply to the credit allowable under §44B (targeted jobs/new jobs credit), which was repealed in 1984. It was replaced by §38/§51 and later work-opportunity credit rules that this section does not implement. The cross-referenced §46(e) and §46(h) are also gone.

judge_2.rationale: Section 44B was repealed, but IRC 52(e) is still in force and still requires rules similar to former 46(e) and (h) for RICs, REITs and cooperatives in computing the section 51 work opportunity credit. So paras (b) and (c)(1) still operate. The mutual-savings rule in para (a) and the pre-1978 rule in (c)(2) are dead.

reader_A.reason: This regulation exclusively addresses limitations on the targeted jobs credit under section 44B, which was repealed in 1996 and replaced by the Work Opportunity Tax Credit, making these rules inapplicable to taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation implements section 44B (the targeted jobs credit), which was repealed in 1984, making all rules in this regulation inoperative for 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The wagering excise tax (§4401) and its territorial-extent rule (§4404) are in force as of March 2025. This rule defines which wagers are taxable in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: The wagering excise tax (IRC 4401) and its territorial-extent rule (4404) are both in force as of March 2025. The regulation's rule on where a wager is treated as placed still applies.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes operative rules for the federal excise tax on wagers under section 4401, which remains an active tax provision with no stated expiration for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation 26 CFR § 44.4404-1 establishes territorial rules for the tax imposed by section 4401, and the evidence confirms that both section 4401 and section 4404 remain in force as of March 2025, meaning these rules continue to operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: 25.2702-1 sets out the scope, effect and exceptions of IRC 2702 (retained interests in trust transfers). Section 2702 and every Code provision it cites are in force at March 2025. The May 19, 1997 split still leaves the post-1997 CRT rule operating.

judge_2.rationale: Section 2702's special valuation rules for transfers in trust (and exceptions such as personal residence trusts) are in force and apply to 2025 gifts.

reader_A.reason: Section 2702 and its implementing regulations governing the valuation of retained interests in trusts are fundamental estate and gift tax provisions that remained in effect for tax years beginning in 2025, with no indication of repeal or material modification to the core rules stated in this section.

reader_B.reason: Section 2702 and this regulation implementing it are confirmed in force as of March 2025, and the valuation rules for retained interests in family trusts continue to apply to taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: 1.934-1 implements IRC 934(a) and (b), the Virgin Islands tax-reduction limit, its exceptions and the computation rules. Section 934 is in force in 2025. A stale 7651(5)(B) subdivision cite does not defeat the operative rules, and the text limits none of them to an ended period.

judge_2.rationale: IRC 934(a) and (b) limit Virgin Islands reductions of tax liability and are in force. The reg sets out current rules, and its text limits no rule to an ended period.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly states it applies for taxable years ending after April 9, 2008, and contains no expiration date, so it operates for 2025 taxable years.

reader_B.reason: The regulation 26 CFR § 1.934-1 contains operative rules that apply to taxable years ending after April 9, 2008, and all underlying Code sections cited remain in force as of March 2025 with no sunset provisions stated in the text.

judge_1.rationale: Payments under a qualified educational assistance program are excluded from wages for withholding if they are reasonably expected to be excludable under IRC 127. Section 127 is permanent and in force in 2025. The rule applies to all taxable years beginning after 1978.

judge_2.rationale: The exclusion from wages and withholding for qualified educational assistance under section 127 applies to taxable years after 1978. Section 127 is permanent and in force in 2025.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1978 and states that payments or benefits under a qualified educational assistance program meeting section 127 requirements are not subject to withholding, a rule that remains operative for 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1978 (clearly including 2025), and the underlying section 127 is confirmed in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Paragraph (e) says the section applies only to gifts made before January 1, 1970. The Tax Reform Act of 1969 struck the 681(b) prohibited-transaction rules it relies on, so current 681(b) is only a cross reference. Later gifts go to 25.2522(c)-2.

judge_2.rationale: Paragraph (e) says this section applies only to gifts made before January 1, 1970, and points to 25.2522(c)-2 for later gifts. It has no effect on 2025 transfers.

reader_A.reason: Section (e) explicitly limits application to gifts made before January 1, 1970, and directs to § 25.2522(c)-2 for later gifts, making it inapplicable to any taxable year beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly limits its applicability to gifts made before January 1, 1970, with reference to a separate regulation for later gifts, making it entirely inapplicable to taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The section implements IRC 6404(g), which suspends interest and penalties when the IRS does not send notice within 36 months. Section 6404(g) is in force in 2025, and paragraphs (a) through (c) have applied since 2011. Only the reportable-transaction and closed-transaction details are tied to past dates, and a stale 6229 cite does not change that.

judge_2.rationale: IRC 6404(g) suspension of interest and penalties when the IRS does not give timely notice (36-month period) is in force. The rules apply to individual returns filed now. The past dates appear only in examples and effective-date provisions.

reader_A.reason: This regulation establishes ongoing procedural rules for suspension of interest and penalties when the IRS fails to provide timely notice of increased tax liability, effective since 2011, with no stated expiration date, making them applicable to taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The core suspension rule in 26 CFR § 301.6404-4(a) establishes a general, non-sunset provision requiring the IRS to suspend interest and penalties when it fails to timely notice a taxpayer within 18 or 36 months; all underlying statutory provisions it cites (26 U.S.C. § 6404(g), § 6411, § 6223, etc.) remain in force as of March 2025 and would apply to 2025 tax years.

judge_1.rationale: The section gives rules for voluntary income tax withholding on third-party sick pay under IRC 3402(o) (Form W-4S), which is in force in 2025. Stale cites (1954 Code, 105(d)(4), the 1981-only option) do not remove the request, amount, duration and payor rules that still apply.

judge_2.rationale: Voluntary withholding on third-party sick pay under IRC 3402(o)(1)(C) (Form W-4S) remains in force. The 'on or after May 1, 1981' language only sets a start date. The stale 105(d) references do not eliminate the core request-and-withhold rule.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes procedures for requesting income tax withholding on sick pay under IRC Section 3402(o) with no stated expiration date or limitation to specific years, so these procedures remain operative for taxable years beginning in 2025 unless superseded by subsequent legislation or regulations.

reader_B.reason: The regulation authorizes payees to request withholding on sick pay with no stated expiration date; while one narrow 1981-only exception has expired, the core provisions remain operative as underlying statutes are in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The information-return rule covers only patronage in cooperative taxable years beginning before Jan 1, 1963, and relies on section 522, which was repealed in 1962. Patronage reporting now runs under 6044 and 1.6044-2 and later sections. Nothing here applies to 2025.

judge_2.rationale: 1.6044-1 is limited to patronage occurring in taxable years beginning before Jan 1, 1963. Section 522 was repealed in 1962. Current reporting falls under 1.6044-2 and later sections.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly limits its scope to patronage occurring in taxable years beginning before 1963, which excludes taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation 26 CFR § 1.6044-1 explicitly limits its application to patronage occurring in taxable years beginning before January 1, 1963, which ended long before 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This is a one-time transition rule for recomputing 1957 taxes of life insurance companies after the 1958 accounting change. The ten installments ran from 1960 to 1969. The cited 818(e) subdivisions no longer exist, and 6016 and 6152 were repealed. It has no effect in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: 1.818-6 is a transition rule for recomputing life insurance companies' 1957 tax. It also covers installments due 1960-1969. The provisions it cites (818(e)(3)/(4), 6152, 6016) are gone or repealed, and the rule is entirely limited to past periods.

reader_A.reason: This section is an entirely historical transitional rule for the 1957-1958 accounting change for life insurance companies, with installment payments scheduled to end in 1969, making it effectively inapplicable to taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: This is a transitional rule specific to the 1957-1958 accounting method change for life insurance companies, and the evidence file confirms that its text limits rules to a period that ended before 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Section 3134 (the COVID employee retention credit) applies only to wages paid in 2021 quarters. The recapture rule treats erroneous refunds as underpayments of the 2021 employment taxes, so it is tied to past periods. The IRS may still collect those amounts in 2025, but no 2025 taxable-year credit exists for the rule to apply to.

judge_2.rationale: This section only covers recapture of section 3134 Employee Retention Credits. Those credits are limited to wages paid in 2021 quarters (before 2022). The IRS may still assess erroneous refunds in 2025, but the underpayment belongs to past periods. No rule applies to a 2025 taxable year.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes rules for recapturing erroneously refunded Employee Retention Credits and treating them as tax underpayments, with an applicability date of September 8, 2021 forward and no stated expiration, meaning these recapture and assessment rules continue to operate in taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation (26 CFR § 31.3134-1) contains substantive rules about recapturing erroneously refunded credits under IRC section 3134, with an applicability date of September 8, 2021 and no expiration date stated; the evidence file confirms that all cited statutes remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Sections 4681 and 4682 are still in force: the tax on ozone-depleting chemicals, the tax on imported products, and the floor stocks tax each January 1. The base tax amount under 4681(b)(1)(B) keeps rising each year after 1995. The definitions and tax computations apply to 2025 sales, uses and the Jan 1, 2025 floor stocks.

judge_2.rationale: Sections 4681 and 4682 are in force and still impose the ozone-depleting chemical (ODC) tax and the annual Jan 1 floor stocks tax. The definitions and computation rules still apply to 2025 sales and uses. The stale 4681(b)(1)(C) citation does not change that.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly imposes a floor stocks tax on January 1 of each calendar year after 1989 (including January 1, 2025) and contains ongoing tax rules with no stated expiration date.

reader_B.reason: This regulation imposes taxes on ozone-depleting chemicals with no stated end date, the underlying statutory provisions remain in force as of March 2025 per the evidence file, and the regulation applies to sales, uses, and inventory holdings with no temporal limitation excluding 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This regulation implements the original 1954 section 683 (Applicability of provisions), a transition rule tied to enactment of the 1954 Code. Current section 683 is a different provision, on trusts used as exchange funds. The rule only separates pre-1954 years from later ones, so no 2025 computation depends on it.

judge_2.rationale: 1.683-1 is a transition rule for moving from the 1939 Code to the 1954 Code. It covers taxable years beginning after 1953 and ending after Aug 16, 1954. Subchapter J now applies through the 1986 Code, so this rule has no remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly states that Part I of subchapter J applies to estates, trusts, and beneficiaries for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1953 and ending after August 16, 1954, which encompasses all taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation establishes that Part I of Subchapter J applies to estates and trusts for taxable years beginning after December 31, 1953 and ending after August 16, 1954, which encompasses all 2025 taxable years, and the evidence confirms the underlying section 641 is still in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Section 512(c) (a tax-exempt partner includes its share of a partnership's unrelated business income) and section 512(b) are in force. The look-through rule and the rule for mismatched taxable years apply to exempt organizations for 2025.

judge_2.rationale: 1.512(c)-1 says an exempt organization's share of a partnership's unrelated trade or business income counts toward its UBTI. Sections 511 and 512(c) are still in force, and nothing in the rule limits it to a past period.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes fundamental rules requiring exempt organizations that are partnership members to include their share of partnership income and deductions from unrelated business activities in computing unrelated business taxable income—a core provision of the unrelated business income tax regime that remains in effect with no stated expiration date or limitation to specific years.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's core rule about computing unrelated business taxable income for exempt organizations in partnerships is still operative because the underlying statutes it implements (sections 511 and 512(b)) remain in force as of March 2025, with no sunset provision or repeal indicated.

judge_1.rationale: IRC 193 (tertiary injectant deduction) remains in force; the deduction, hydrocarbon limitation, and 263(c) coordination rules still apply. The windfall-profit-tax citations (4993/4996) are stale, but 193(b) still refers to the June 1979 energy regulations, and the Chief Counsel approval route still works.

judge_2.rationale: Section 193 (the tertiary injectant deduction) is still in force (verified in the Code as of March 2025). The deduction timing, the hydrocarbon limit and the 263(c) coordination rules still apply. The cites to repealed windfall profit tax sections 4993/4996 affect only one prong of the definition of tertiary recovery method.

reader_A.reason: Section 193's tertiary injectant deduction provisions were extended only through 2016 and do not appear to apply to taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: Section 193, the statutory basis for this regulation, is in force as of March 2025 per the evidence ledger. The core deduction rule in 26 CFR 1.193-1(a) is unrestricted by any sunset or expiration date and applies to qualified tertiary injectant expenses, allowing this rule to operate for taxable years beginning in 2025. Although some cited regulatory pathways reference non-existent code sections (4996 and 4993), the regulation provides alternative qualifying routes and the fundamental deduction mechanism remains valid.

judge_1.rationale: This is a one-time retroactive election for reacquisitions in taxable years beginning 1958 through Sept. 2, 1964. The election had to be made by Sept. 3, 1965, and the interest rule covers only periods before Sept. 2, 1964. Every rule is tied to a period that has ended.

judge_2.rationale: The election covers only reacquisitions in taxable years beginning after 1957 and before September 3, 1964, and had to be made by September 3, 1965. The limitation-period extensions and interest rules are tied to that election. Every rule is confined to past periods.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly limits all its provisions to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1957 and before September 3, 1964, which excludes any taxable year beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly limits its application to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1957 and before September 3, 1964, and all election procedures had to be completed by September 3, 1965, making this regulation inapplicable to taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The applicability rule that 1.306-1 through 1.306-3 apply on or after June 22, 1954 is open-ended and still controls when the section 306 regulations apply. Section 306 remains in force. Only the part about section 1022 (repealed) is dead.

judge_2.rationale: This section makes the 1.306-1 through 1.306-3 regulations applicable on or after June 22, 1954, with no end date. Section 306 is in force, so the applicability rule still operates. Only the reference to section 1022 (repealed for 2010 carryover basis) is stale.

reader_A.reason: The section states that provisions are applicable 'on or after June 22, 1954' and 'on and after January 19, 2017', indicating continuing applicability through 2025 and beyond without stated termination dates.

reader_B.reason: The section states that provisions §§ 1.306-1 through 1.306-3 are applicable on or after June 22, 1954, which is a rule that continues to operate in 2025 since no end date is specified.

judge_1.rationale: Open-ended applicability dates still govern: 1.148-1 through -11 apply to bonds sold on or after July 8, 1997; the 2016 updates, the 2017 issue-price rule, and the 2019 investment-type property rule apply going forward. The state perpetual-fund guarantee rule in (d)(1) still operates. Section 148 is in force.

judge_2.rationale: Paragraph (a) applies the 1.148 arbitrage regulations to bonds sold on or after July 8, 1997. Paragraphs (k) through (n) set forward-looking dates, and the (d) state guarantee fund rule applies to new issues. Section 148 is in force, so these rules govern bonds and hedges in 2025. The dead 103A cites and past windows don't change that.

reader_A.reason: The regulation contains multiple operative provisions with effective dates extending to and beyond 2025, including the general applicability rule (section a) for bonds sold after July 8, 1997, and arbitrage guidance updates (section k) for bonds sold after October 17, 2016.

reader_B.reason: The section contains operative applicability rules (particularly paragraph (a)) that specify when §§ 1.148-1 through 1.148-11 apply to bonds sold on or after July 8, 1997, which continues to govern bonds in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This is a cross-reference defining gross investment income for purposes of 509(e) by pointing to 1.509(a)-3(m). Section 509(e) and the public-support tests remain in force, so the pointer still operates.

judge_2.rationale: This is a pointer that defines gross investment income under section 509(e) by reference to 1.509(a)-3(m). Section 509(e) and the 509(a)(2) public-support test are still in force, so the definitional rule still applies to exempt organizations.

reader_A.reason: Section 509(e) regulations defining gross investment income for tax-exempt organizations remain in effect for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation states a rule defining gross investment income by reference to § 1.509(a)-3(m), and since its authority section (26 U.S.C. § 7805) remains in force as of March 2025 with no evidence of repeal or supersession in the provided evidence, this definitional rule continues to operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The special lien for estate tax deferred under section 6324A, for section 6166 elections, is still in force: the lien property, maximum value, priority, and definition rules apply to estates deferring tax today. Only the 6166A references are dead.

judge_2.rationale: The special lien in lieu of bond under section 6324A for estate tax deferred under section 6166 is still in force (6324A, 6166, 6325 and 6621 are all current). The stale references to 6166A don't touch the lien-property, priority and definition rules, which still apply to current deferrals.

reader_A.reason: Section 6166 installment payment elections for estates remain operative in 2025, and this regulation establishes the rules for the special lien mechanism (section 6324A) available under that current statute.

reader_B.reason: Section 6166 remains in force and deferrals made under it can extend into 2025, meaning the regulation's provisions for liens, property designation, and deferral administration still operate, though evidence suggests certain rule limitations ended before 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Paragraph (a) restates IRC 1503(a), which is still in force: consolidated-return tax is computed under the section 1502 regulations. Paragraph (b), on Western Hemisphere trade corporations (section 921 repealed) and the old additional tax, is dead, but paragraph (a) still applies.

judge_2.rationale: Paragraph (a) says that consolidated return tax is determined under the §1502 regulations. That tracks the current §1503(a), which is in force. Paragraph (b), covering WHTCs under §921 (repealed) and the old surtax increase, is obsolete. Paragraph (a) still states an operative rule.

reader_A.reason: The general rule in part (a) directing that consolidated returns follow section 1502 regulations remains operative for 2025, though the Western Hemisphere trade corporation limitation in part (b) is obsolete.

reader_B.reason: The general rule in subsection (a) requires consolidated return tax to be computed according to section 1502 regulations, which remains in force as of March 2025, and the regulation text contains no time limits on its rules.

judge_1.rationale: The functional-currency rules under section 985 (dollar QBUs, the hyperinflation rule, the facts-and-circumstances test) apply to tax years beginning after 1986, amended in 2024. Sections 985-989 are in force. Only the noncontrolled section 902 corporation reference is stale.

judge_2.rationale: §1.985-1 sets the rules for choosing the functional currency of a taxpayer or QBU under §985, which is in force. It applies to taxable years beginning after 1986 and was amended as recently as 2024. The pre-1994 hyperinflation rule and the §902 reference are stale, but the core rules still apply.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986 with no termination date, making its rules operative for 2025 tax years, including requirements for determining functional currency.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to all taxable years beginning after December 31, 1986, which includes 2025; the general functional currency determination rules in paragraphs (b) and (c) have no expiration dates, though some specific provisions for transition and hyperinflationary periods ended before 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This section implements IRC 1251 (farm recapture property and the excess deductions account), which was repealed in 1984. Every rule depends on section 1251(c)/(d), so nothing in it still applies.

judge_2.rationale: The section covers exceptions to recapture of excess deductions account gain under §1251, which was repealed in 1984, and it depends on §182, repealed in 1986. With the underlying recapture regime gone, none of its rules has any effect.

reader_A.reason: Section 1251 and its statutory exceptions for gifts, transfers at death, and certain corporate transactions remain operative provisions in the tax code that would apply to dispositions of farm recapture property in 2025, though application is rare because such property is now 50+ years old.

reader_B.reason: Section 1251 and all its major subsections that this regulation explains were repealed in 1984, making the regulation inapplicable to current taxable years.

judge_1.rationale: The duty to collect the section 4261 air transportation tax on orders paid outside the U.S. applies to amounts paid on or after January 19, 2021. Sections 4261, 4291 and 6672 are in force.

judge_2.rationale: The duty to collect the §4261 air transportation tax on prepaid orders paid outside the U.S. applies to amounts paid on or after Jan 19, 2021. Sections 4261, 4291 and 6672 are all in force, so the rule applies in 2025.

reader_A.reason: 26 CFR § 49.4263-1 establishes a duty to collect tax on transportation payments made outside the United States, with an applicability date of "on and after January 19, 2021" with no stated expiration, so this rule continues to operate for amounts paid during taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's applicability date is January 19, 2021, applies to future amounts paid, and all cited Code sections remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This is the section 1103(g) election for bank holding company divestitures under sections 1101-1103 and 6158. Those sections are repealed (6158 in 1990, and sections 1101-1103 are repealed as well), so the election has no remaining effect.

judge_2.rationale: The section implements the bank holding company election under §1103(g), which ties to §§1101-1103 and 6158. All of those provisions are repealed. No 2025 taxpayer could make or apply this election, so the section has no remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: The regulation states multiple substantive operating rules (how elections are made, application to tax returns, irrevocability, certification requirements) that are not explicitly sunset and would technically apply to any bank holding company making such elections in a 2025 taxable year, despite the rule's focus on pre-June 30, 1968 activities.

reader_B.reason: The regulation implements sections 1101, 1103, and 6158 of the Internal Revenue Code, all of which have been repealed (with section 6158 repealed in 1990), making the regulatory rules inoperative for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This section defines 'nonforfeitable' for section 411(a) vesting and sets out the exceptions (death, lost beneficiary, multiemployer plans, certain matching contributions). Section 411 is in force. The section 412(c)(8) citation is stale, but the core rules still apply.

judge_2.rationale: §1.411(a)-4 defines nonforfeitability under §411(a), which is in force, along with the special rules for death, multiemployer plans, lost beneficiaries and matching contributions. Qualified plans apply these rules today. The stale citation to §412(c)(8), now §412(d)(2), does not stop the section from operating.

reader_A.reason: This regulation establishes fundamental, permanent nonforfeitability requirements for accrued pension benefits under IRC Section 411, which are core provisions of tax law that continue to apply to all pension plans in all taxable years including those beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation defines nonforfeitability rules under section 411(a), which the evidence confirms is in force as of March 2025, and the text itself contains no sunset dates or temporal limitations on its rules.

judge_1.rationale: The electronic-filing rule for Form 1042 applies to returns for taxable years ending on or after Dec 31, 2023, so it covers 2025. Section 6651 and the chapter 3 withholding rules it relies on are still in force.

judge_2.rationale: The rule requires electronic filing of Form 1042 by withholding agents that file 10 or more returns. It applies to returns for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2023, so it covers 2025. Sections 6011 and 6651 are in force.

reader_A.reason: The regulation's applicability date clause explicitly states the rules apply to withholding tax returns required to be filed for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2023, which includes all taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's applicability clause explicitly states "The rules of this section apply to withholding tax returns required to be filed for taxable years ending on or after December 31, 2023," which encompasses all taxable years beginning in 2025, and the underlying statutory provision (section 6651) remains in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The per-barrel fee under OCSLA Amendments of 1978 sec. 302(d) paid into the Offshore Oil Pollution Compensation Fund. Oil Pollution Act of 1990 sec. 2004 repealed Title III of those amendments, so the fee no longer exists. The Code sections it cites (7502, 7503, 7805) being in force does not revive it.

judge_2.rationale: This is a per-barrel fee under OCSLA Amendments of 1978 §302(d) for the Offshore Oil Pollution Compensation Fund. The Oil Pollution Act of 1990 (§2004) repealed Title III of the OCSLA Amendments, so the fee is no longer imposed. It also has no connection to a taxable year.

reader_A.reason: The regulation clearly states multiple enforceable rules regarding offshore oil fee collection that became effective in 1979, and absent any indication of repeal or suspension within the text itself, these rules would presumptively still operate in 2025, though definitive confirmation would require external verification.

reader_B.reason: The regulation became effective July 25, 1979 with no expiration date, and evidence confirms its underlying IRC provisions (sections 7502, 7503, 7805) remained in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: This section implements the old mutual insurance company rules in IRC 821-824 (as enacted in 1962). The Tax Reform Act of 1986 repealed them. The ledger confirms 821(f), 822(c)(6)/(f), 823 and 824(d) do not exist in the March 2025 Code, so the dividend definition has nothing left to apply to.

judge_2.rationale: The regulation implements sections 821-824, the mutual insurance company regime (underwriting loss, protection against loss account), which the Tax Reform Act of 1986 repealed. The ledger confirms none of those sections exist at 119-4. Today's property and casualty insurers fall under §832, so this rule has no remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: This regulation contains operational rules for how insurance companies must account for dividends to policyholders for tax purposes, including rules for both cash and accrual accounting methods; these structural rules contain no expiration date and were last updated in 2019, indicating they remain current for 2025 tax years.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's substantive rules apply exclusively to sections 821-824 of the IRC, which no longer exist in the Code as of March 2025; the lone cross-reference to section 561 is not itself a rule that operates.

judge_1.rationale: Section 1402(g) (the reg's 1402(h), later renumbered) still exempts religious-group members from self-employment tax through Form 4029. The approval conditions and the rule on how long an exemption stays in effect still apply, even though the 1967/1968 filing-deadline and refund rules are past.

judge_2.rationale: The self-employment tax exemption for members of religious sects opposed to insurance is still in the Code (now §1402(g), with the application rules in 1402(h) per the ledger), and taxpayers still file Form 4029. The approval conditions, when the exemption takes effect, and the filing deadline for years ending after 1967 still apply, even though (c)(1) and (g) are limited to past periods.

reader_A.reason: Section (f)(1) explicitly states that an approved exemption application applies to "all taxable years beginning after December 31, 1950," which encompasses years beginning in 2025, so long as the individual continues to meet the sect membership and conscientious opposition requirements.

reader_B.reason: Paragraph (f) states exemptions are effective for all taxable years beginning after December 31, 1950, directly encompassing 2025, and section 1402(h) remains in force as of March 2025, though referenced subdivisions (1)(C), (1)(D), and (2) no longer exist in the Code.

judge_1.rationale: Section 7704(b) is in force. The reg's definitions of established securities market, secondary market and its safe harbors (private placement, 2% trading) apply to taxable years beginning after 1995. Only the transition rule in (l)(4) cites the repealed 708(b)(1)(B).

judge_2.rationale: Section 7704(b) is in force. The tests for when a partnership is publicly traded (established securities market, secondary market, safe harbors, private placement, the 2% rule) apply to current taxable years. The stale cite to 708(b)(1)(B), repealed by TCJA, affects only a transition-rule sentence.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1995, which includes all taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 1995 per paragraph (l)(1), which includes 2025; section 7704(b) remains in force (March 2025 per evidence); and the regulation contains no time-limit language ending its rules.

judge_1.rationale: Depreciation basis is still the section 1011 adjusted basis (IRC 167(c)). Treas. Reg. 1.168(i)-4(b) cross-references this section's rule for property converted to business use: the lower of fair market value or adjusted basis. That rule still applies in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: Section 1011 is in force, and section 167(c) (formerly 167(g)) still bases depreciation on adjusted basis. The rule that property converted to business use takes the lower of fair market value or adjusted basis still applies, including under MACRS through §1.168(i)-4(b).

reader_A.reason: The regulation states fundamental depreciation principles—using adjusted basis under section 1011 and applying fair market value if less than adjusted basis for converted property—that lack expiration dates and remain foundational to the tax code for any taxable year including 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's depreciation basis rules remain operative for 2025 taxable years because section 1011 is confirmed in force and the regulation itself has not been repealed or sunset.

judge_1.rationale: Rules govern the time for filing corporate declarations of estimated tax under section 6016, which was repealed in 1968. Corporations no longer file declarations; they only make estimated payments under 6655. Paragraphs (a) and (c)(1) are limited to pre-1964 years, and paragraphs (b) and (c)(2) depend on declarations that no longer exist.

judge_2.rationale: The section times corporate declarations of estimated tax for short years, which depend on section 6016(a). Section 6016 was repealed in 1968, and corporations no longer file declarations: section 6655 governs estimated tax installments. The dated amendment rules have no remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: Section (b) applies to short taxable years beginning after December 31, 1963, which includes 2025, establishing filing deadlines for estimated tax declarations.

reader_B.reason: The regulation cites section 6016(a), which was repealed in 1968 according to the evidence; section (a) explicitly applies only to years beginning on or before December 31, 1963, and section (b) applies to years after 1963 but is contingent on meeting requirements under the now-repealed section 6016(a); the evidence confirms that "the text limits at least one rule to a period that ended before 2025."

judge_1.rationale: Sections 562(c) and 565 are in force. The preferential-dividend bar on the dividends-paid deduction still applies to personal holding companies, non-publicly-offered REITs and similar entities. The 1954 dates appear only in examples.

judge_2.rationale: Section 562(c)'s preferential-dividend limit on the dividends-paid deduction is still in force (it still applies to REITs, non-publicly-offered RICs and personal holding companies). The rule that any preference disallows the deduction for the whole distribution still applies.

reader_A.reason: This regulation states foundational rules under Section 562(c) regarding the dividend paid deduction—specifically, that shareholders of the same stock class must be treated equally and preferential dividend distributions disqualify the deduction. These are general structural rules that would remain operative for taxable years beginning in 2025 absent legislative repeal of the underlying IRC section.

reader_B.reason: The regulation states rules about dividend deduction requirements and preferential dividend treatment, and the underlying statutes it cites (sections 562(b), 562(c), and 565) are confirmed to be in force as of March 2025 by the evidence ledger.

judge_1.rationale: Section 381(c)(19) and 170(d)(2) are in force. The post-1962 rules still govern how an acquiring corporation takes over and deducts a transferor's excess charitable contributions: the 5-year carryover, same-numbered preceding years treated as one year, and no deduction in the year of transfer. The 5% figure is stale (the limit is now 10%), but the method still applies.

judge_2.rationale: Section 381(c)(19) and 170(d)(2) are still in force. Paragraph (a)(2), for transferor years beginning after 1961, is the current rule: the acquiring corporation carries over the transferor's excess contributions (5-year carryover). The pre-1962 and 1962 transition rules are dead, but the general rule still operates.

reader_A.reason: IRC Section 381(c)(19) and its implementing regulations continue to require acquiring corporations to account for excess charitable contributions in modern transactions, including those beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: Section (c)(3) provides ongoing rules for acquiring corporations in section 381(a) transactions occurring after 1962, with no explicit termination date, making it operative for 2025 taxable years where acquisitions occurred in recent periods.

judge_1.rationale: Section 503(e) is in force and still defines when a debt obligation acquired by a trust described in 503(a)(1) (501(c)(17)/(18) and certain governmental or church plans) is not treated as a loan without adequate security. The text limits none of its rules to past periods. The citation to 503(a)(1)(B) is stale.

judge_2.rationale: Section 503(e) is still in force (only 503(d) was repealed), as is 503(b)(1). Section 503 still applies to 501(c)(17)/(18) organizations and to 401(a) trusts referred to in 4975(g)(2)/(3). The rules on how an obligation is acquired and on the 25% limit remain operative even though the examples are dated.

reader_A.reason: Section 503 of the IRC was effectively eliminated by ERISA and subsequent tax law changes, making this regulation that interprets section 503(e) non-operative for 2025 taxable years.

reader_B.reason: The evidence confirms that all cited Code provisions are in force as of March 2025, and the regulation text contains no language limiting its rules to an ended time period.

judge_1.rationale: Section 958(a) indirect ownership through foreign entities, and the domestic-partnership aggregate rule in paragraph (d), which applies to foreign-corporation taxable years beginning on or after Jan 25, 2022, both operate for 951, 951A and 956 in 2025. Only a few cross-references (such as those to 955) are to repealed provisions.

judge_2.rationale: Section 958(a) direct and indirect ownership rules for subpart F and GILTI are still in force, and so are 951, 956, 958(b) and 318. The repealed 955 references and the 960(a)(1) reference are only stale parentheticals. The proportional attribution rules through foreign entities still apply in 2025.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to taxable years beginning on or after January 25, 2022 (covering 2025) with no stated sunset date, and governs CFC ownership attribution rules that remain in effect.

reader_B.reason: The regulation contains stock ownership attribution rules in sections (a)-(c) with no stated expiration dates, and section (d) explicitly applies to taxable years beginning January 25, 2022 onward, which includes 2025; the underlying statutes cited (sections 951, 958, 956, 957, 951A) remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Section 521 is in force, and the rules for farmers' cooperative exemption still apply: patron treatment, the nonmember limits, the 15% nonproducer purchasing limit and the 8% stock-dividend cap. Stale items such as the reference to section 522 (repealed 1962), Form 1028 and district directors do not remove the substantive rules.

judge_2.rationale: Section 521 (farmers' cooperative exemption) and section 1388 are still in force. The exemption requirements (proportionate patronage distributions, record-keeping) still apply. Only the cross-reference to section 522 (repealed 1962) is stale.

reader_A.reason: IRC Section 521 and these implementing regulations remain in full force and effect in 2025, governing the tax-exempt status of qualifying farmers' cooperative associations.

reader_B.reason: Section 521, which this regulation implements and explains, remains in force as of March 2025 (per the evidence ledger), the regulation contains no sunset provisions or time-limited rules, and the substantive requirements for farmers' cooperative exemption status that it prescribes continue to apply to taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §53.4945-1 implements the section 4945 excise taxes on private foundation taxable expenditures (foundation tax, manager tax, and second-tier taxes). Section 4945 and the provisions it cites are in force as of March 2025, with no sunset.

judge_2.rationale: Section 4945 taxes on private foundation taxable expenditures remain in force. The rates and caps stated in the reg are stale (now 20%/5%, $10k/$20k after PPA 2006), but the definitions of knowing, willful and correction, joint and several liability, and the taxable period still apply.

reader_A.reason: The regulation imposes specific excise tax rules under IRC Section 4945 on private foundations and their managers (e.g., 10% tax on taxable expenditures, 2.5% tax on foundation manager agreement), which remain active provisions of the Internal Revenue Code with no sunset or repeal indicated in the text.

reader_B.reason: All Code sections cited by this regulation are confirmed in force as of March 2025, making the regulation's substantive rules operative for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §1.545-2 sets the section 545(b) adjustments used to compute undistributed personal holding company income (taxes, charitable contributions, NOL, dividends-received deduction, and so on). Sections 541 and 545 are in force. Some cross-references (902, 545(b)(8)/(9)) and some dated rules are stale, but the core adjustments still apply.

judge_2.rationale: The personal holding company tax (541) and 545(b) adjustments remain in force. The deductions for federal and foreign income taxes, the post-1969 charitable contribution limits, disallowed special deductions, the NOL rule, the net capital gain deduction and the property expense limit still apply. Some paragraphs are obsolete (pre-1970 rules, 601, 902, pre-1934 debt).

reader_A.reason: This section provides rules for calculating undistributed personal holding company income under IRC section 545, which still applies to corporations classified as personal holding companies under section 541 in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation contains multiple time-unlimited rules applicable to 2025 taxable years, including deductions for Federal income taxes (section a), charitable contributions for years after 1969 (section b(2)), and restrictions on special deductions and net operating loss deductions (sections c and d), all with cited Code sections that remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §1.892-5(a)(3) defines 'entity' for section 892(a)(2)(B), which covers controlled commercial entities of foreign governments. It applies on or after Jan 14, 2002, and section 892 is in force, so the definition still applies in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: Defines 'entity' for 892(a)(2)(B), which is in force (controlled commercial entity rules for foreign governments). It applies on or after Jan 14, 2002, with no end date.

reader_A.reason: Section 1.892-5(a)(3) provides a definitional rule for "entity" that applies on or after January 14, 2002, with no repeal or sunset provision indicated, clearly operating for 2025 tax years.

reader_B.reason: The regulation § 1.892-5(a)(3) defines "entity" to include corporations, partnerships, trusts, and estates for purposes of section 892(a)(2)(B), with an effective date of "January 14, 2002 on or after," and the underlying statute section 892(a)(2)(B) remains in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §1.451-2 states the constructive receipt doctrine under section 451, a foundational rule for cash-method taxpayers that still applies. The only stale citation is the cross-reference to repealed section 1232(a)(3).

judge_2.rationale: The constructive receipt doctrine under section 451 is a core, current rule for cash-method taxpayers. Only the incidental cross-reference to repealed 1232(a)(3) is stale.

reader_A.reason: The constructive receipt of income doctrine established in 26 CFR § 1.451-2 is a foundational principle of federal income tax law with no stated expiration or sunset date and remains in effect for all taxable years including those beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: 26 CFR § 1.451-2 establishes foundational rules about constructive receipt of income that are not limited to any ended period and continue to apply for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §301.7605-1 sets reasonable time and place rules for IRS examinations under sections 7602 and 7605(b), which are in force. It is procedural and not limited to past periods. The cross-reference to repealed section 556 is incidental.

judge_2.rationale: Implements 7602/7605(b), both in force: reasonable time and place of examination, 10-day summons appearance, one inspection per taxable year. It is effective for examinations after 1993 with no end date. The repealed 556 cross-reference is incidental.

reader_A.reason: The regulation establishes permanent procedural rules for IRS examinations with effective dates in 1993 and 1970, contains no sunset or expiration provisions, and therefore continues to operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation establishes procedural rules governing IRS examination time, place, and frequency that lack temporal limitations and apply to examinations of returns for taxable years beginning in 2025; the evidence confirms the underlying statutes remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: Single-employer defined benefit plans moved to section 404(o) under the PPA. Section 404(a)(1)(A) still gives multiemployer plans clauses (i)-(iii), including 10-year amortization of past service credits. The reg's rules on plan year vs. taxable year, 10-year bases and the full funding limit still govern those plans, even though its section 412 cross-references are stale.

judge_2.rationale: 1.404(a)-14 computes the 404(a)(1)(A) deductible limit. PPA 2006 moved single-employer plans to 404(o) and restructured 412, so many cross-references are stale. But 404(a)(1)(A)(i)-(iii) remain in force for multiemployer plans (funded under 431), and the rules on plan year vs. taxable year, 10-year bases and the full funding limit still apply to those deductions.

reader_A.reason: The regulation contains general, non-time-limited methodology rules for computing deductible pension plan contributions that would continue to apply to 2025 taxable years, though some specific computational references may have been modified by subsequent tax legislation.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's core substantive provisions in paragraphs (c) through (k) provide rules for computing deductible contributions under section 404(a)(1)(A) for defined benefit plans; these provisions lack explicit time limitations and rely on statute sections (404, 412, 401, 403, 446) confirmed still in force as of March 2025, whereas the time-limited rules (e.g., paragraph (l) for "plan years beginning before April 22, 1981") are historical transitional provisions.

judge_1.rationale: Basis rules for exchanges under §§1031, 1035(a), 1036(a), 1037(a) remain in force (1031 still covers real property exchanges). Only the §1002 citation is stale; the basis rules still apply in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: The basis rules for property received in §1031, 1035, 1036 and 1037 exchanges (substituted basis, boot adjustments, allocation) still apply. §1031(b)-(d) and §§1035-1037 are in force. A stale cite to repealed §1002 in one paragraph does not change the operative rules.

reader_A.reason: Section 1031 exchanges for real estate remain operative in 2025, and this regulation's basis computation rules continue to apply to such exchanges under current tax law.

reader_B.reason: The regulation 26 CFR § 1.1031(d)-1 establishes rules for determining basis of property acquired in tax-free exchanges, and the evidence confirms that all substantive underlying code sections it relies on (1031, 1035(a), 1036(a), 1037(a), 1016, 1031(b), and 1031(c)) remain in force as of March 2025, with no sunset dates stated in the regulatory text.

judge_1.rationale: Implements the old §30 qualified electric vehicle credit, which was repealed in 2014 and covered only vehicles placed in service before 2007. Recapture applies only within 3 years of placement in service, so it cannot occur in 2025. The §1245 tie-in exists only for credits allowed long ago.

judge_2.rationale: The Code shows the old §30 qualified electric vehicle credit repealed by Pub. L. 113-295 (2014). It covered only vehicles placed in service before 2007, so every 3-year recapture window closed long ago. The §1245 rule could in theory reach a 2025 sale of such a vehicle, but it has no practical remaining effect.

reader_A.reason: Section 30 electric vehicle credits are not available for taxable years beginning in 2025, having been superseded by section 30D; the regulation's recapture procedures only apply when the underlying credit existed.

reader_B.reason: The section 1245 application rule in paragraph (b)(7) can still operate when a vehicle previously qualified under repealed section 30 is sold in 2025, treating the prior credit as depreciation under section 167 for section 1245 purposes.

judge_1.rationale: The §45V clean hydrogen credit, with its 5x multiplier for prevailing wage and apprenticeship under §45(b)(7)-(8), is in force as of March 2025. The reg applies to facilities placed in service in taxable years ending after June 25, 2024.

judge_2.rationale: The increased (x5) §45V credit for meeting prevailing wage and apprenticeship rules applies to facilities placed in service in taxable years ending after June 25, 2024. The Code shows §45V and §45(b)(7)-(8) in force. The 2025 legislation only ended the credit for construction beginning after 2027.

reader_A.reason: The regulation's applicability date explicitly applies to qualified clean hydrogen production facilities placed in service in taxable years ending after June 25, 2024, covering taxable years beginning in 2025, with ongoing substantive requirements for prevailing wage, apprenticeship, and recordkeeping that continue to operate.

reader_B.reason: 26 CFR § 1.45V-3 explicitly applies to qualified clean hydrogen production facilities placed in service in taxable years ending after June 25, 2024 (applicability date in paragraph (c)), which includes taxable years beginning in 2025, and the evidence confirms all cited underlying statutory provisions remain in force as of March 2025.

judge_1.rationale: §404(a), (b) and (d) are in force. The 2 1/2-month rule separating deferred compensation from current compensation still governs when employers may deduct. Only the §463 vacation-pay reference and the 1984-86 transition rule are dated.

judge_2.rationale: The 2½-month rule in Q&A-2, which decides whether pay counts as deferred compensation under §404(a),(b),(d), is still applied to year-end bonuses and accruals. §404 is in force. Only the §463 vacation-pay cross-reference and the 1984-86 transition rule in Q&A-2(d) are dead.

reader_A.reason: The regulation's effective date clause explicitly states it applies to taxable years ending after July 18, 1984, with no stated expiration, meaning these rules still govern compensation deferral treatment for 2025 taxable years.

reader_B.reason: Section 404(b) is confirmed in force as of March 2025, and the regulation establishes the substantive "2 1/2 month period" rule for determining deferred compensation that applies to compensation in any taxable year unless specifically repealed.

judge_1.rationale: §1398 and §465 are in force. The rules on how at-risk losses pass to and from the bankruptcy estate apply to cases commencing on or after Nov 9, 1992. The flagged '554(a)' is a Title 11 (Bankruptcy Code) cite, not an IRC cite.

judge_2.rationale: §1.1398-2 covers how §465 at-risk losses pass between an individual debtor and the bankruptcy estate in chapter 7/11 cases. It applies to cases commencing on or after Nov 9, 1992, and §§465 and 1398 are in force. The ledger's '554(a) repealed' is wrong: that cite is to title 11, not the IRC.

reader_A.reason: The regulation's effective date provision (section f(1)) specifies it applies to bankruptcy cases commencing on or after November 9, 1992, which includes any cases commencing during taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to bankruptcy cases commencing on or after November 9, 1992, which includes 2025, contains no sunset dates, and its underlying section 465 provisions remain in force.

judge_1.rationale: Defines 'less developed country' under §955(c)(3). The 2017 TCJA repealed §955 along with the rules on withdrawing previously excluded subpart F income from qualified investment in less developed countries, so the definition no longer has any effect.

judge_2.rationale: The less-developed-country definition exists only for old §955 (withdrawal of previously excluded subpart F income from qualified investment in LDCs). The Code confirms §955 was repealed by Pub. L. 115-97 §14212 (2017), and the LDC exclusions it served were repealed earlier. Nothing uses the designation in 2025.

reader_A.reason: This regulation implements the Subpart F provisions (sections 951-964) involving less-developed country designations, which were substantially superseded by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act's Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) rules effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017.

reader_B.reason: Section 955(c)(3), which provides the statutory authority for the designation and termination procedures in subsections (b) and (c), was repealed in 2017, eliminating the regulatory framework's operative authority.

judge_1.rationale: Interest-waiver rules for tax increases caused by the 1955 repeal of IRC 1954 secs. 452 and 462 (both repealed). The rules turn on payments due before Dec 15, 1955, and interest under 1939 Code sec. 3779. Every rule is limited to past periods.

judge_2.rationale: 1.9000-6 waives interest on tax increases caused by the 1955 repeal of sections 452 and 462, for amounts paid by Dec 15, 1955 and for 1954-55 periods. It applies only to that past period, and 1939 Code 3779 no longer exists.

reader_A.reason: This regulation is entirely focused on transitional provisions related to the 1955 repeal of IRC sections 452 and 462, with all specific deadlines and requirements tied to dates in 1955 (particularly December 15, 1955), and no provisions that would operate prospectively for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: All provisions are time-limited transitional rules addressing the 1955 repeal of sections 452 and 462, with explicit date limits (December 15, 1955, and periods prior to June 16, 1955) that ended decades before 2025.

adjudicated.rationale: 1.274-14 implements 274(l), which disallows deductions for employer-provided commuting transportation. 274(l) is in force at 119-4, with no sunset like 274(a)(4)'s. Para (d) applies the section to taxable years beginning on or after Dec 16, 2020, so a 2025 year is covered.

judge_1.rationale: PLACEHOLDER

judge_2.rationale: 1.274-14 implements 274(l), which disallows deductions for commuting expenses. 274(l) is in force, and the section applies to taxable years beginning on or after Dec 16, 2020, which includes 2025.

reader_A.reason: The section's applicability date states it applies to taxable years beginning on or after December 16, 2020, with no stated termination date, so the disallowance rules for commuting expenses continue to operate for 2025.

reader_B.reason: 26 CFR § 1.274-14 explicitly applies to taxable years beginning on or after December 16, 2020, and all cited Code provisions remain in force as of March 2025, so the regulation's rules on disallowance of commuting and transportation expense deductions operate for 2025 tax years.

judge_1.rationale: Definitions for section 2801 (tax on covered gifts and bequests from covered expatriates). Section 2801 is in force, and paragraph (n) makes the section apply to covered gifts and bequests received on or after January 1, 2025.

judge_2.rationale: 28.2801-2 defines terms for the 2801 tax on covered gifts and bequests. 2801 is in force, and the section applies to covered gifts or bequests received on or after Jan 1, 2025, so it operates for 2025.

reader_A.reason: The section's applicability date (paragraph n) explicitly states "This section applies to covered gifts or covered bequests received on or after January 1, 2025," meaning all the definitional rules operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to covered gifts or covered bequests received on or after January 1, 2025, and all cited statutory provisions are in force as of March 2025, confirming these definitional rules operate for taxable years beginning in 2025.

judge_1.rationale: The weight-based rates are obsolete: since 2004, section 4071(a) taxes tires on load capacity (9.45 cents per 10 lbs above 3,500 lbs). Section 4071 is still in force, though. The manufacturer-liability rule in (c) and the open-ended rule in (d) (recapping or retreading is not taxable manufacture, but imported foreign-recapped tires are taxable), effective for sales on or after 1984, still apply in 2025.

judge_2.rationale: The weight-based rates are obsolete: the 2004 AJCA changed 4071(a) to a load-capacity basis. But the 4071 tire tax still runs until Oct 1, 2028. Para (c), under which the manufacturer is liable on sale or on delivery to its own retail outlet (4071(b)), and para (d), which exempts recapped or retreaded tires except imported ones, still apply.

reader_A.reason: Section 48.4071-1(a)(2) and subsection (b)(2) impose excise tax on highway vehicle tires sold after December 31, 1983, with rates and rules that explicitly apply on or after January 1, 1984, remaining operative for taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation contains rules for tax on highway vehicle tires sold after December 31, 1983 (section (b)(2) and section (d) regarding recapped tires) with no stated expiration date, and the underlying statute (26 U.S.C. § 4071) is confirmed in force as of March 2025, meaning these rules operate for 2025 taxable years.

judge_1.rationale: The business-lease regime under old section 514 was replaced by the debt-financed property rules in the Tax Reform Act of 1969. Current 514(f) covers only personal property leased with real property, and 514(g) is now a regulations grant; neither is 'business lease indebtedness'. The cited 514(f)(2)(B) no longer exists. The definition has no remaining operation for 2025.

judge_2.rationale: The 1969 Tax Reform Act (Pub. L. 91-172) repealed the old 514 'business lease' regime and replaced it with unrelated debt-financed income rules. Old 514(f)/(g) business lease provisions no longer exist, and current 514(f)(2)(B) does not exist. The rule has no effect for 2025.

reader_A.reason: The regulation states current definitional and computational rules for determining business leases under IRC section 514 that are not limited to past years and would apply to taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: The regulation's core definitional and computational rules for business leases lack explicit expiration dates and reference IRC sections that remain in force as of March 2025, though evidence shows at least one cited subdivision no longer exists.

judge_1.rationale: Consistent-basis requirement under section 1014(f), issued by T.D. 9991 in September 2024. It applies to property acquired from decedents whose estate tax returns are filed after September 17, 2024. Sections 1014 and 6035 are in force, so the rule governs basis for 2025 taxable years.

judge_2.rationale: 1.1014-10 consistent-basis rules implement 1014(f), which is in force. They apply to property acquired from a decedent whose estate tax return is filed after Sept 17, 2024, so they govern basis reporting in 2025.

reader_A.reason: The regulation explicitly applies to property acquired from a decedent when the decedent's Federal estate tax return is filed after September 17, 2024, which encompasses estates with returns filed in 2025 and taxable years beginning in 2025.

reader_B.reason: 26 CFR § 1.1014-10 applies to property from decedents whose estate tax returns are filed after September 17, 2024, making the consistent basis requirement rules operative for taxable years beginning in 2025.
